cards.q: Define global, local and strict minimizers of min f(x) over S. How do they imply each other?
pts: Global min: f(x) ≥ f(x*) for all x ∈ S; strict if f(x) > f(x*) for all x ∈ S, x ≠ x*.
Local min: there is ε > 0 with f(x*) ≤ f(x) for all x ∈ B(x*, ε) ∩ S; strict local min uses < for x ≠ x*.
Chain: strict global ⇒ global ⇒ local, and strict global ⇒ strict local ⇒ local.
A strict global minimizer is automatically unique.
cards.pit: Global does not imply strict: for a constant function every point is a global min and none is strict.

cards.q: Gradient and Hessian of bᵀx, xᵀBx and ½xᵀAx (A symmetric)?
pts: ∇(bᵀx) = b and ∇(xᵀx) = 2x.
∇(xᵀBx) = (B + Bᵀ)x and ∇²(xᵀBx) = B + Bᵀ for a general square B.
For f = ½xᵀAx + bᵀx + c with A = Aᵀ: ∇f = Ax + b and H = A.
cards.pit: ∇(xᵀBx) = 2Bx only when B is symmetric — the slide's derivative table drops this condition.

cards.q: State the first-order necessary condition (FONC) with its hypotheses.
pts: f is differentiable at x*.
x* is a local minimizer of the unconstrained problem min over ℝⁿ (an interior point, so every direction is allowed).
Then ∇f(x*) = 0; such a point is called a stationary point.
cards.pit: The converse is false: f = x³ has f′(0) = 0, but 0 is neither a min nor a max.

cards.q: What are the three essential moves in a rigorous proof of FONC?
pts: Fix any direction d; for small t > 0, x* + td is in the ball, so f(x* + td) − f(x*) ≥ 0.
Divide by t > 0 (inequality keeps direction) and let t ↓ 0 using the o(t) Taylor remainder: ∇f(x*)ᵀd ≥ 0 for every d.
Choose d = −∇f(x*): −‖∇f(x*)‖² ≥ 0, hence ∇f(x*) = 0.
cards.pit: The slide ends with “∇f(x*)ᵀd = 0 and d ≠ 0, so ∇f(x*) = 0” — false for a single d (g = (1,0), d = (0,1)). The argument must hold for all d.

cards.q: What can FONC do, and what can it not do?
pts: Can: rule out every non-stationary point and reduce the search to solving ∇f(x) = 0 (n equations, n unknowns).
Cannot tell a min from a max: f and −f have the same stationary points.
Cannot rule out saddle points.
May be vacuous: f = x₁ − 2x₂ has no stationary point at all (unbounded below).
cards.pit: Existence is a separate question: eˣ is strictly convex with infimum 0 but has no minimizer and no stationary point.

cards.q: Why does FONC fail for min x over [0, 1] at x* = 0, and for f = |x| at 0?
pts: On [0, 1], x* = 0 is a boundary point: only feasible directions d ≥ 0 are allowed, so the proof only gives ∇f(x*)ᵀd ≥ 0 for feasible d (f′(0) = 1 ≠ 0).
That “no feasible descent direction” condition is the seed of the KKT conditions.
f = |x| has a strict global min at 0 but is not differentiable there, so the hypothesis of FONC fails (one-sided derivatives ±1).
cards.pit: Non-smooth losses such as the hinge loss have the same issue at the kink — the reason subgradients exist.

cards.q: Define a convex set and give standard examples.
pts: C is convex if x, y ∈ C and λ ∈ [0, 1] imply λx + (1 − λ)y ∈ C (the whole segment stays in C).
Examples: ℝⁿ, ∅, half-spaces {aᵀx ≥ β}, balls, affine sets {Ax = b}, the PSD cone.
Affine sets contain the whole line through two points, not just the segment (any λ ∈ ℝ works).
cards.pit: A union of convex sets is not convex in general: [0, 1] ∪ [2, 3] misses the midpoint 1.5.

cards.q: Which operations preserve convexity of sets? Why is an LP feasible set convex?
pts: Any intersection (arbitrary index set) of convex sets is convex.
Scaling βC and the Minkowski sum C₁ + C₂ are convex.
A polyhedron {Ax ≤ b} is an intersection of half-spaces, so it is convex — this covers LP feasible sets.
Sublevel sets {g(x) ≤ 0} of convex g are convex, so {gᵢ(x) ≤ 0 ∀i, Ax = b} is convex when every gᵢ is convex.

cards.q: Define a convex function. Why must the domain be convex first?
pts: f(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≤ λf(x) + (1 − λ)f(y) for all x, y ∈ S, λ ∈ [0, 1] — the chord lies above the graph.
Strictly convex: strict inequality whenever x ≠ y and λ ∈ (0, 1). f is concave if −f is convex.
The definition evaluates f at λx + (1 − λ)y, so it only makes sense when S is convex.
cards.pit: “Is 1/x convex?” is ill-posed on ℝ∖{0}; on (0, ∞) it is convex.

cards.q: When is f(x) = ½xᵀAx + bᵀx + c (A symmetric) convex or strictly convex? Why?
pts: Identity: λf(x) + (1 − λ)f(y) − f(λx + (1 − λ)y) = ½λ(1 − λ)(x − y)ᵀA(x − y).
So f is convex ⇔ A ⪰ 0, and strictly convex ⇔ A ≻ 0 — no Hessian argument needed.
Portfolio variance xᵀQx is convex because a covariance matrix is PSD (xᵀQx = Var(xᵀr) ≥ 0); strictly convex iff no riskless combination exists.
cards.pit: Necessity: if vᵀAv < 0 for some v, choose x − y = v and the identity turns negative.

cards.q: Which operations preserve convexity of functions?
pts: Sum f₁ + f₂ is convex; strictly convex if at least one term is.
αf with α > 0 keeps (strict) convexity.
Composition g∘f is convex if f is convex and g: ℝ → ℝ is convex and nondecreasing on the range of f.
Also (not on the slides): affine pre-composition g(Ax + b) and pointwise max of convex functions — needed for hinge and logistic losses.
cards.pit: Drop “nondecreasing” and it fails: g(y) = e^{−y}, f = x² gives e^{−x²}, whose second derivative at 0 is −2.

cards.q: State the Hessian test for convexity with all its hypotheses.
pts: C is non-empty, open and convex, and f ∈ C²(C).
f is convex on C ⇔ H(x) ⪰ 0 for all x ∈ C.
H(x) ≻ 0 for all x ∈ C ⇒ f strictly convex — but not conversely: x⁴ is strictly convex with f″(0) = 0.
cards.pit: The slide says “strictly convex iff PD”, which is wrong in the ⇒ direction. “Open” matters too: x₁² − x₂² restricted to the line x₂ = 0 is convex although H is indefinite.

cards.q: How do you check positive definite vs positive semidefinite?
pts: PD: all leading principal minors > 0, or all eigenvalues > 0.
PSD: all principal minors ≥ 0 — not only the leading ones — or all eigenvalues ≥ 0.
cards.pit: Leading minors ≥ 0 does not give PSD: diag(0, −1) has leading minors 0 and 0 but is not PSD.

cards.q: State the “local = global” theorem for convex problems and the key step of its proof.
pts: Convex problem: S is a convex set and f is convex on S. Then every local minimizer is a global minimizer.
If f is strictly convex, the minimizer is the unique, strict global minimizer.
Proof: for y outside the ball, take z = λ′x* + (1 − λ′)y with 1 − λ′ = ε/‖y − x*‖, so z lies on the ball and in S.
Then f(x*) ≤ f(z) ≤ λ′f(x*) + (1 − λ′)f(y); divide by 1 − λ′ > 0 to get f(x*) ≤ f(y).
cards.pit: Both convexities are needed: (x − 2)² on S = [−1, 0] ∪ [1, 3] has a local min at 0 that is not global.

cards.q: State the gradient inequality and what it implies for stationary points.
pts: f differentiable on open convex C: f convex ⇔ f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ(y − x) for all x, y ∈ C.
The tangent plane is a global under-estimator; strict convexity ⇔ strict inequality for y ≠ x.
Corollary: if f is convex and ∇f(x*) = 0, then x* is a global minimizer (strict if f is strictly convex).
So for differentiable convex f on ℝⁿ, FONC is necessary and sufficient.
cards.pit: On a constrained convex S the right condition is ∇f(x*)ᵀ(y − x*) ≥ 0 for all y ∈ S, not ∇f(x*) = 0.

cards.q: Least squares min ½‖Xw − y‖²: convexity, solution and when it is unique.
pts: ∇f = Xᵀ(Xw − y) and H = XᵀX ⪰ 0, so f is always convex.
If X has full column rank, XᵀX ≻ 0 and the unique minimizer is w* = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy (normal equations).
Optimality means the residual is orthogonal to the columns of X: Xᵀr = 0.
Rank-deficient X: still convex (local = global) but infinitely many minimizers; ridge (XᵀX + γI) restores uniqueness.
cards.pit: The slides say “full row rank” — backwards. A tall regression matrix can never have full row rank; what is needed is full column rank.

cards.q: State SONC and SOSC. What is the gap between them?
pts: SONC: if x̄ is a local min and f is twice differentiable, then ∇f(x̄) = 0 and H(x̄) ⪰ 0.
SOSC: if ∇f(x*) = 0 and H(x*) ≻ 0, then x* is a strict local min.
SOSC is local only — one PD Hessian says nothing global (x³ − x² − 4x − 6 has a strict local min but is unbounded below).
Gap: when H(x*) is PSD and singular, neither decides — x⁴ is a min, x³ is neither.
cards.pit: x₁² + x₂⁴ and x₁² − x₂⁴ both have H(0) = diag(2, 0), yet one is a strict min and the other a saddle: look along the null direction.

cards.q: What is a saddle point, and how do you detect one?
pts: A stationary point that is neither a local min nor a local max: every neighbourhood has points with larger and with smaller f.
Test: ∇f(x*) = 0 and H(x*) indefinite ⇒ saddle point.
A symmetric matrix is indefinite ⇔ it has a positive and a negative eigenvalue.
cards.pit: A PSD but singular Hessian can still be a saddle (x₁² − x₂⁴ at 0); indefiniteness is sufficient, not necessary.

cards.q: Classify the stationary points of f(x) = x³ − x² − 4x − 6.
pts: f″ = 6x − 2: at x₊ = (1 + √13)/3, f″ = 2√13 > 0 ⇒ strict local min.
At x₋ = (1 − √13)/3, f″ = −2√13 < 0 ⇒ strict local max.
No global min: f → −∞ as x → −∞.
cards.pit: The slide prints ∇f = 3x² − 2x − 2, which does not match the stationary points it quotes; the correct derivative is 3x² − 2x − 4.
